l: fear of the Lord, The Book of Job
s: The fear of the Lord is declared by God to man to be wisdom. It is paired with the statement that departing from evil is understanding.

l: poor and needy (those Job helped), The Book of Job
s: The poor who cried, the fatherless with no helper, and the one ready to perish were delivered by Job. The perishing one's blessing came on Job, and the widow's heart was caused to sing for joy. Job was a father to the needy and investigated the cause of those he did not know.

l: men (Job's listeners), The Book of Job
s: has_attitude_toward Job [waited for him as for the rain] Young men saw Job and hid themselves, the aged rose and stood, and princes and nobles fell silent, hands on their mouths and tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths. They listened, waited, and kept silent for his counsel, did not speak again after his words, and waited for him as for the rain. When they lacked confidence he smiled on them, and they did not reject the light of his face.

l: Job's former prosperity and honor, The Book of Job
s: Job's remembered past prosperity and honor in Chapter 29: abundance with steps washed in butter and rock pouring oil, God's protective watch, a respected seat at the city gate, esteem from all ranks, blessings from those he helped, and expectations of lasting glory and many days.

l: Job's suffering and affliction, The Book of Job
s: Job's affliction, described in Chapter 30, is relentless suffering: days of affliction seize him, his soul is poured out, bones are pierced and burn with heat, with no rest at night. His skin blackens and peels, terrors chase his honor, and he mourns, companion to jackals and ostriches.

l: Elihu, The Book of Job
s: Elihu is a Buzite, son of Barachel of the family of Ram, and the youngest voice in the records: younger than Job's three friends. He waited to speak out of deference to their age, then grew angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the three friends for condemning Job without finding an answer. He holds that understanding comes from the Spirit of the Almighty, not from age, and that God made him from clay, giving him the same standing before God as Job. He claims sincerity, refuses flattery and partiality, and says he fears his Maker. Across five chapters his speech unfolds. In chapter 32 he explains his delay and resolves to give his opinion. In chapter 33 he addresses Job directly, says God is greater than man, and desires to justify Job or teach him wisdom. In chapter 34 he calls on wise men to judge, argues that God does no wickedness, and accuses Job of speaking without knowledge and multiplying words against God. In chapter 35 he answers Job and his companions, arguing that human righteousness does not affect God and that Job speaks empty words. In chapter 36 he asks patience, claims to speak on God's behalf as one perfect in knowledge, defends God's justice, and ends praising God's power over the weather.

l: three friends (Job's three friends), The Book of Job
s: The three friends cease to answer Job, who remains righteous in his own eyes. Elihu is angry at them because they found no answer yet condemned Job. He says they are amazed, have no word left to say, and should not claim that God, not man, will refute Job.

l: wrath (Elihu's wrath), The Book of Job
s: Elihu's wrath is kindled against Job because Job justified himself rather than God. It is also kindled against the three friends because they found no answer yet condemned Job. It is mentioned again when Elihu sees that the three men have no answer.

l: age and wisdom, The Book of Job
s: has_relationship not necessarily linked [Elihu's claim] Elihu says he first thought days and many years should teach wisdom, which is why he held back as the younger man. He then asserts that a spirit in man, the Spirit of the Almighty, gives understanding, and that it is not the great who are wise nor the aged who understand justice.

l: man, The Book of Job
s: is_formed_out_of clay Man is portrayed as often paying no attention when God speaks. God opens his ears, withdraws him from his purpose, hides pride from him, and keeps his soul from the pit and his life from perishing by the sword. If he is shown what is right and ransomed, he is restored, prays and is received, sees God's face with joy, and sings before men of his sin.

l: God's communication through dreams and visions, The Book of Job
s: God's communication through dreams and night visions occurs when deep sleep falls on men. Though man ignores his speaking, God opens their ears and seals instruction, aiming to withdraw man from his purpose, hide pride, and keep his soul from the pit and death by the sword.

l: suffering and chastening of a man on his sickbed, The Book of Job
s: A man on his sickbed is chastened with pain and constant strife in his bones; he loses appetite for food, his flesh wastes away and bones protrude, and his soul draws near the pit and the destroyers.

l: Job's claim of innocence, The Book of Job
s: Job's claim of innocence: he asserts he is clean, disobedience-free and innocent, yet God counts him an enemy. In Chapter 33 the speaker rebuts that Job is not just, since God is greater than man.

l: restoration and redemption of a man, The Book of Job
s: A topic of a man's restoration and redemption by God. When an angel-interpreter, one among a thousand, shows him what is right, God graciously delivers him from the pit, finding a ransom. His flesh grows fresher than a child's, he prays, sees God's face with joy, regains righteousness, confesses his sin publicly, and declares his life will see light. God does this twice, even three times.

l: wise men (Elihu's audience), The Book of Job
s: Elihu addresses them as wise men and men of understanding with knowledge, asking them to listen, to test his words as the palate tastes food, and to choose with him what is right. He expects them to agree that Job speaks without knowledge and that his words lack wisdom.

l: God's justice, The Book of Job
s: is_characterized_by impartiality [applies to princes, rich and poor alike] Elihu insists that God's justice is beyond question: far be it from God to do wickedness, and he will not pervert justice. He gives each man the result of his work, shows no partiality between princes, the rich, and the poor, and needs no further inquiry into a man before judging. Elihu asks whether one who hates justice could govern, and says God overturns the wicked and hears the cries of the afflicted.

l: Job's complaint against God (Job's claim of righteousness), The Book of Job
s: Job's complaint, as restated by Elihu, claims Job is righteous, God has taken away his right, his wound is incurable despite no disobedience, and serving God profits nothing. Elihu rejects it, insisting God cannot act unjustly and calling Job's words rebellion.

l: righteousness, The Book of Job
s: benefits man [may profit a son of man] Elihu says Job claims that his righteousness is more than God's. He argues that a righteous person gives God nothing and that God receives nothing from his hand, and that righteousness profits only other people, a son of man.

l: sin and wickedness, The Book of Job
s: affects man [can hurt a fellow human, not God] Elihu says that sinning and multiplying transgressions have no effect against God and do nothing to him. He says a person's wickedness may hurt other people, and that the pride of evil men is the reason the cries of the oppressed go unanswered.

l: the wicked, The Book of Job
s: The wicked, godless in heart, lay up anger and do not cry for help when God binds them. God does not preserve their lives; they die in youth among the unclean, perishing by the sword without knowledge.

l: the righteous, The Book of Job
s: is_exalted_by God [set forever with kings on the throne] God does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, and he sets them with kings on the throne forever, exalted. If they are bound in fetters and afflictions, he shows them their work and their proud transgressions, opens their ears to instruction, and commands them to turn from iniquity. If they listen and serve him, they spend their days in prosperity and their years in pleasures.

l: rain and clouds (God's weather), The Book of Job
s: God draws up the drops of water, which distill as rain from his vapor, and the skies pour it down abundantly on man. No one can understand the spreading of the clouds or the thunderings of his pavilion. By these means he judges the people and gives food in abundance, and the noise of the storm tells about him, as the livestock also do.

l: thunder and lightning (God's voice), The Book of Job
s: God's voice sounds as thunder and roars under the whole sky, and his lightning goes to the ends of the earth. The thunder holds nothing back when heard, and God thunders marvelously. The speaker's heart trembles at it, and he calls on listeners to hear the noise of the voice.

l: wild donkey, The Book of Job
s: A wild donkey set free by God, given wilderness and salt land as home; it scorns the city's tumult and driver's shouting, and ranges the mountains seeking every green thing.

l: wild ox, The Book of Job
s: The wild ox is an animal of great strength but untameable: it refuses to serve at a feeding trough or be harnessed in the furrow, so it cannot be trusted with labor, seed, or grain.

l: ostrich, The Book of Job
s: The ostrich is a bird whose wings wave proudly, yet she leaves her eggs on the earth, heedless that feet or wild animals may crush them. She is harsh to her young and fearless, lacks wisdom because God deprived her, but scorns horse and rider when she lifts herself.

l: horse, The Book of Job
s: A powerful horse with a quivering mane, leaping like a locust and snorting awesomely. He paws the valley, exults in strength, mocks fear, never flinches from the sword, and answers the trumpet with 'Aha!', smelling battle from afar.

l: eagle, The Book of Job
s: The eagle is a high-nesting bird that, unprompted, dwells on a cliff stronghold. With far-seeing eyes it spies prey from there, and its young suck up blood, so it is found wherever the slain are.

l: behemoth, The Book of Job
s: Behemoth is a creature made by the LORD along with Job. It eats grass like an ox and has immense strength in its thighs and belly muscles, with bones like bronze tubes and limbs like iron bars. Called the chief of the ways of God, it is given its sword by its maker. It rests under lotus trees and willows, stays unafraid when a river overflows, and is fed by mountains. The text asks whether anyone could capture it.

l: judgment of God, The Book of Job
s: The LORD asks Job whether he will even annul his judgment or condemn him so that Job may be justified. This frames Job's earlier argument as a challenge to God's judgment, which Job is asked to answer for.

l: friends (Job's three friends), The Book of Job
s: The LORD tells Eliphaz that his wrath is kindled against him and his two friends because they did not speak rightly of him as Job did. They take seven bulls and seven rams to Job and offer a burnt offering, and Job prays for them so the LORD will not deal with them according to their folly.

l: burnt offering (offered by Job's friends), The Book of Job
s: The LORD commands Job's friends to take seven bulls and seven rams and offer them as a burnt offering. They do as commanded, and Job prays for them, after which the LORD accepts Job.

l: Job's restored prosperity, The Book of Job
s: Job's restored prosperity follows his prayer for his friends: the LORD gives him twice as much as before, including fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, oxen, donkeys, seven sons and three daughters, while relatives comfort him and give gifts.

l: Job's repentance, The Book of Job
s: is_expressed_by Job [in dust and ashes] Job says he had heard of the LORD by the hearing of the ear but now his eye sees him. Therefore he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes, having uttered things he did not understand.

l: The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: This document is a five-chapter sequence of laments over the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of its people, expressed through shifting voices and addressed largely to the LORD. Zion, personified as the daughter of Zion, a widow, and a ruined city, is the central figure, alongside the LORD, whose anger is portrayed as the cause of the devastation, and the people, priests, prophets, and enemies. Chapter 1 pictures Jerusalem solitary and betrayed, with Judah in captivity and adversaries mocking her. Her affliction is attributed to the LORD because of her transgressions. She speaks in her own voice, confesses rebellion, and asks that her enemies be treated as she has been. Chapter 2 describes the Lord as an enemy throwing down strongholds, the tabernacle, altar, and sanctuary. King, priest, and prophets are despised, children faint from hunger, and false prophets failed to expose iniquity. It ends with a call to cry out to the Lord and a prayer to look at the slain and starving. Chapter 3 turns to one man who has seen affliction, walled in and shot with arrows. He then finds hope in the LORD's mercies, new every morning, urges returning and confessing, recalls being cast into a dungeon and redeemed, and asks for his enemies to be repaid. Chapter 4 recounts the siege's aftermath: once precious sons and nobles starve, mothers have boiled their children, and the sins of prophets and priests are blamed. The anointed of the LORD is captured. Edom is told the cup will pass to her, while Zion's punishment is accomplished and she will not be carried into captivity again. Chapter 5 closes as a communal prayer asking the LORD to remember their reproach. They list lost inheritance, servants ruling them, abuse, mourning, and desolate Zion where foxes walk. They confess sin, affirm that the LORD reigns forever, and plead for restoration, ending with the fear that he has utterly rejected them and is very angry.

l: Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: Jerusalem is a city once called the perfection of beauty and the joy of the whole earth, now fallen from greatness. The records portray her as a widow and slave, unclean for grievous sin, with no comforter, despised by nations and betrayed by lovers who became enemies. Her adversaries prosper, her sanctuary was entered by nations, and the LORD afflicted her in fierce anger for her many transgressions. Chapter 1 shows her solitary and weeping, confessing rebellion and asking the LORD to see her distress. Chapter 2 shows her virgins and children suffering, passersby mocking her, and the speaker asking what could comfort her.

l: LORD, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The LORD is the central figure across these five lamenting chapters, portrayed as a God who both afflicts and shows mercy. Early on he acts in fierce anger against Jerusalem and Zion for her transgressions: sending fire, spreading a net, treading her as in a wine press, and, like an enemy, covering Zion with a cloud, swallowing dwellings, casting off his altar and sanctuary, and scattering prophets and priests. This destruction is presented as fulfilling a word he commanded in days of old, done without pity. Jerusalem acknowledges he is righteous and asks him to look and see her affliction. In the middle, the speaker who has seen affliction turns to hope: the LORD's loving kindness and faithfulness do not fail, his mercies are new every morning, he is the speaker's portion, and he is good to those who wait for him. He does not cast off forever, does not afflict willingly, and is the Most High from whose mouth evil and good come. The speaker recalls being heard from the dungeon and redeemed, and asks for judgment on his enemies. Later the wrath is accomplished, kindling a fire in Zion that devoured its foundations, and the people are scattered. The records close with the community asking him to remember, noting he remains forever with a throne from generation to generation, begging him to renew their days, yet ending with the fear that he has utterly rejected them and is very angry.

l: Jacob, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: has_dwellings swallowed up [by the Lord without pity] All the dwellings of Jacob are swallowed up without pity, and the Lord burns up Jacob like a flaming fire that devours all around.

l: adversary and enemy (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: Jerusalem's adversaries and enemies are a hostile group who prosper and are exalted, with the Lord having raised their horn and given them Zion's palaces. They mock her desolations, rejoice in her trouble, and claim to have swallowed her up. They enter the sanctuary the LORD forbade to nations, and breach her gates, which even the kings of the earth thought impossible. Pursuing swifter than eagles, they hunt her people through mountains, wilderness and streets, while Jerusalem asks that their wickedness come before the LORD.

l: people of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The people of Jerusalem, starving and sighing, trade their treasures for bread; priests and elders perish seeking food, princes weaken like pasture-less deer, and young men and virgins are crushed and taken into captivity.

l: captivity (exile of Judah), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: Judah has gone into captivity because of affliction and great servitude, dwelling among the nations and finding no rest, with persecutors overtaking her. Her young children, virgins, and young men are described as having gone into captivity before the adversary.

l: sins of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: described_as yoke bound by the LORD's hand [knit together on her neck] The chapter says Jerusalem grievously sinned, became unclean, and did not remember her latter end, with her filthiness in her skirts. The LORD afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions, which are pictured as a yoke bound by his hand on her neck, and she confesses that she rebelled against his commandment.

l: daughter of Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The daughter of Zion is a personified community under the Lord's anger: covered with a cloud, her wall marked for destruction, wrath poured out like fire. Her elders sit silent in mourning, her breach is incurable as the sea, and she is told to cry out day and night.

l: Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: Zion is a place, portrayed as a city and mountain under divine judgment. The Lord causes its assemblies and Sabbath to be forgotten, and elders mourn. A fire devours its foundations, yet its punishment is declared accomplished and captivity ended. It closes desolate, with ravished women and foxes roaming its mountain.

l: Israel, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: Israel is a group whose beauty the Lord casts from heaven to earth; in fierce anger he cuts off its horn, swallows it and its palaces, and acts as its enemy.

l: prophets and priests (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The prophets and priests of Jerusalem are blamed for the city's ruin because of their sins and iniquities, chiefly shedding the just's blood within it. They wander blind through the streets, so blood-polluted that none can touch their garments, and the people withhold respect.

l: children and infants (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The children and infants of Jerusalem suffer famine in the besieged city. They faint in the streets, beg mothers for grain and wine, and thirst and lack bread that no one breaks for them. Zion is urged to pray for their lives. It culminates in the horror of women eating or boiling their own children during the destruction.

l: destruction of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The destruction of Jerusalem is portrayed as the Lord's act in his anger. Strongholds, palaces, walls, the tabernacle and sanctuary are cast down, with famine, sword slaughter, and a fire devouring Zion's foundations. Prophets' and priests' sins are blamed. Women resort to cannibalism of children, mourning fills Judah, and the people say their end is near and their days fulfilled.

l: famine, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: is_worse_than the sword [those killed by hunger fare worse than those killed by sword] Hunger is portrayed as worse than the sword: those killed by the sword are better off than those who pine away for lack of the fruits of the field. Its effects include thirsty infants, children without bread, delicately raised people in desolation, withered skin, and mothers boiling their children.

l: the speaker (the man who has seen affliction), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: A speaker who has suffered affliction under the LORD's wrath is mocked by his people, dwelling in darkness, walled in, broken, and hunted by baseless enemies. His strength and expectation perish, yet recalling the LORD's mercies restores hope. He calls on the LORD from a dungeon, is told not to fear, is redeemed, and asks judgment on his enemies.

l: the speaker's affliction, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: includes bitterness and wormwood The affliction is portrayed as the LORD's doing: aged flesh, broken bones, bitterness, heavy chains, blocked paths, and arrows in the kidneys. The speaker's soul remembers it and is bowed down, and he asks the LORD to remember it. It is not presented as endless, since the LORD does not afflict willingly and will have compassion.

l: hope in the LORD's mercies and faithfulness, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: is_grounded_in the LORD's loving kindnesses [recalled to mind] The speaker turns to hope by recalling that the LORD's loving kindnesses keep us from being consumed and that his mercies are new every morning. He affirms that great is the LORD's faithfulness, that the LORD is good to those who wait for him, and that it is good to hope and quietly wait for his salvation.

l: enemies (the speaker's enemies), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The speaker's enemies are a hostile group who open their mouths wide against the people, chase him without cause, cut off his life in a dungeon, cast a stone on him, plot all day and mock him in song. The LORD has seen this and will repay and destroy them.

l: speakers (the lamenting community), The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The speakers are a lamenting community who confess their sin and describe their ruin. Early on they are mocked, made refuse among the peoples, and admit they have transgressed and rebelled and are unpardoned. They are then called cruel like ostriches, with iniquity greater than Sodom, and famine blackens their skin. The lament deepens into losses: inheritance given to strangers, orphaned children and widowed mothers, water and wood bought at a price, relentless pursuers, rule by servants with no deliverer, and hands given to Egypt and Assyria for bread. Joy has turned to mourning and the crown has fallen. They acknowledge their fathers' iniquities and their own sin, and end by asking the LORD to turn them and renew their days.

l: sons of Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The sons of Zion, once precious like fine gold, are now esteemed as common earthen pitchers; their nobles, once pure and ruddy, have become blacker than coal, withered, skin clinging to bones.

l: Edom, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: Edom's daughter, dwelling in the land of Uz, is told to rejoice, but the cup will pass to her; she will be drunken and naked, and the LORD will uncover her sins.

l: sin and iniquity, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The speakers say their fathers sinned and are no more, and that they bear their fathers' iniquities. They also confess, 'Woe to us, for we have sinned!', linking the fallen crown and their suffering to sin.

l: desolation and suffering of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah
s: The text lists the suffering: loss of inheritance, orphanhood, paid-for water and wood, pursuit, famine, sword danger, skin blackened like an oven, and rule by servants. Women in Zion and the cities of Judah were ravished, princes were hanged by their hands, young men carried millstones, children stumbled under wood, and the elders' gate-seat and the young men's music ceased. Joy turned to mourning, and Zion's mountain lies desolate.

l: The Book of Ezekiel
s: This is the book of Ezekiel, in 48 chapters: the account of Ezekiel, a priest and son of Buzi, who is among the Judean captives by the river Chebar in the Chaldeans' land. It centers on the LORD, who commissions Ezekiel as a prophet, watchman and living sign to a rebellious Israel, and on the fate of Jerusalem, Israel and the surrounding nations. It opens with Ezekiel's vision of the LORD's glory on a sapphire throne above four living creatures and wheels full of eyes (ch. 1). He is commanded to eat a scroll of lamentation, is hardened against a stubborn people, and is appointed watchman, made mute until the LORD opens his mouth (2-3). Through sign-acts such as a besieged tile, lying on his sides, scarce bread, a shaved head and an acted exile, and through oracles, the LORD announces Jerusalem's coming siege, famine, sword and exile for idolatry, bloodshed and false prophecy (4-7, 12-24). A visionary tour of the temple shows abominations there; the LORD's glory leaves the temple and the city, and a man in linen marks those who grieve (8-11). Chapters 14-23 add the parables of the vine, the foundling bride, the eagles, the lions, the two sisters Oholah and Oholibah, and a teaching on individual responsibility (18). On the day Babylon besieges Jerusalem, Ezekiel's wife dies and he may not mourn (24). Judgments follow on Ammon, Moab, Edom, the Philistines, Tyre and its prince, Sidon, and Egypt and Pharaoh, with Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon as the LORD's instrument (25-32). After a fugitive reports Jerusalem's fall, Ezekiel's mouth is opened and he is again named watchman (33). The tone then turns to hope. The LORD condemns Israel's false shepherds and promises David as one shepherd (34), judges Edom (35), and promises a new heart, his Spirit, and a land like Eden (36). The valley of dry bones revives, and Judah and Joseph are joined as one nation under David with an everlasting covenant (37). Gog of Magog's invasion ends in his defeat and the nations see the LORD's glory (38-39). The last chapters (40-48) give a detailed vision of a restored temple, measured by a guide. The LORD's glory returns through the east gate, and the chapters set out rules for the priests of Zadok, the prince, offerings and feasts. A river flows from the temple and heals the sea, and the land is divided among the tribes. The book ends with the city named 'The LORD is there.'

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Ezekiel is a priest, son of Buzi, living among the captives by the river Chebar in the land of the Chaldeans (at Tel Aviv), in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity. He is called by the LORD through visions of God, and is addressed throughout as 'son of man'. He is sent as prophet and appointed watchman to the rebellious house of Israel, to speak the LORD's words whether they listen or not. The records follow his career from call to ongoing commission. In the opening chapters he sees the glory of the LORD, is raised by the Spirit, eats a scroll, and has his forehead made hard like a diamond so he can face a hostile people. He sits overwhelmed for seven days among the captives, and is warned he will be made mute until the LORD opens his mouth. He then enacts signs: portraying Jerusalem's siege on a tile, lying 390 days on his left side and 40 on his right to bear the iniquity of Israel and Judah, eating rationed bread and water, and, after protesting he has never been unclean, being allowed cow's dung for baking. He shaves his hair and beard with a sword and divides it to symbolize Jerusalem's fate, and is told to prophesy against the mountains of Israel. Later, seated with the elders of Judah, he is lifted by the Spirit in visions to Jerusalem, shown abominations, and sees the twenty-five men at the east gate; when Pelatiah dies he cries out for the remnant, then is carried back to the captives and tells them all. He is called a sign to the house of Israel, acting out exile by bringing out baggage and digging through a wall. He prophesies against false prophets, including prophesying women, receives elders who come to him, judges the elders and the bloody city, and sighs and wails over the coming sword of the king of Babylon. People mock him as a speaker of parables. A pivotal moment comes when his wife dies in the evening and, at the LORD's command, he does not mourn, again becoming a sign; his muteness will end when the escapee comes. Finally he laments over Tyre and prophesies against Pharaoh and Egypt, with a promise that his mouth will be opened among the house of Israel.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The LORD (Lord GOD) is the God of Israel who speaks to and commissions Ezekiel, the priest and prophet, called 'son of man.' The records open with his hand on Ezekiel by the river Chebar and his glory seen above the cherubim. He sends Ezekiel to the rebellious house of Israel, appoints him watchman, and has him enact sign-acts. What matters most is a repeated pattern: the LORD judges Israel for idolatry and abominations, acts for the sake of his holy name, and does it all so that people 'will know that he is the LORD.' In the first half he is against Jerusalem and the mountains of Israel. He brings the sword, destroys high places, breaks the staff of bread, and shows no pity. He refuses inquiry from idolatrous elders and opposes false prophets and faithless shepherds. He insists he judges each person according to his ways, takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and calls Israel to turn and live. His glory then leaves the house and city, rising from the cherub and standing on the mountain east of the city. He remains a sanctuary to the exiles for a little while. He recounts having chosen Israel, given statutes and Sabbaths, and covenanted with Jerusalem, and he charges Oholah and Oholibah with idolatry. He announces that he will profane his sanctuary and will not spare or repent. He then turns against the nations: Ammon, Moab, Edom, the Philistines, Tyre, Sidon, Pharaoh and Egypt, and Mount Seir. He sets Nebuchadnezzar and the sword against them. The tone then shifts to restoration. He declares himself shepherd of his scattered flock, judging between sheep and sheep and making a covenant of peace. He promises to gather Israel into their land, give a new heart and spirit, a heart of flesh in place of stone, and pour out his Spirit. He brings dry bones to life and makes an everlasting covenant of peace. He sets his sanctuary among them, sanctifies Israel, and opposes Gog, whom he strikes down so his holy name is no longer profaned. The records close with his glory filling the restored house, where he will dwell among Israel forever. The east gate stays shut because he entered by it. He sets rules for priests, princes, offerings, and the division of the land he swore to Israel's fathers. The city is finally named 'The LORD is there.'

l: the exiles (Ezekiel's brothers), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The exiles are Ezekiel's brothers and relatives, the whole house of Israel, told by Jerusalem's inhabitants to stay far from the LORD. The LORD scattered them among nations as captives in Chaldea, becomes their temporary sanctuary, promises to gather them and give Israel's land; Ezekiel relays the vision.

l: cherubim, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The cherubim are four winged living creatures seen by the river Chebar, each with four faces (man, lion on the right, ox on the left, eagle), four wings, human hands under the wings, and straight calf-like feet that sparkle like burnished bronze. Eyes cover their bodies, backs, hands and wings. Their appearance is like burning coals and torches, and each has a whirling wheel beside it. They go straight forward without turning, led by the spirit. In Chapter 1 they emerge from a fiery cloud, running like flashes, with wings sounding like great waters and the voice of the Almighty. In Chapter 10 the narrator identifies them as the same creatures; they stand at the right of the house, one hands fire to the man clothed in linen, and they mount up with the wheels and stop at the east gate of the LORD's house.

l: wheels (beside the living creatures), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The wheels are four beryl-like wheels, each a wheel within a wheel, standing beside the living creatures (cherubim) in the vision. Their high, dreadful rims are full of eyes all around. They travel in four directions without turning. Most importantly, they go, stand and lift up together with the creatures because the spirit of the living creature is within them. Chapter 1 introduces them on the earth beside each creature; Chapter 10 repeats the description with the cherubim and names them "the whirling wheels."

l: sapphire throne (above the cherubim), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A throne resembling sapphire stone, located above the crystal-like expanse over the creatures' heads, bearing a likeness of a man seated on it above.

l: man-like figure (on the throne), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A man-like figure seated on the throne above the expanse, glowing metal with fire within from the waist up and fire from the waist down, ringed by rainbow-like brightness; Ezekiel identifies this as the likeness of the LORD's glory.

l: visions of God, The Book of Ezekiel
s: occurs_at river Chebar The heavens are opened and Ezekiel sees visions of God, in the thirtieth year, fourth month, fifth day, among the captives by the river Chebar. The visions include the stormy wind and fiery cloud, the four living creatures, the wheels, the expanse, the throne and the man-like figure in brightness.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The house of Israel is portrayed as a collective people, repeatedly called a nation of rebels and a rebellious house, who have transgressed against the Lord together with their fathers to this day. They are described as impudent, stiff-hearted, obstinate and hard-hearted, with eyes and ears that neither see nor hear, and the LORD says they will not listen to Ezekiel because they will not listen to him. The records open with Ezekiel being sent to them, particularly the captives, whether they hear or refuse, so that they will know a prophet has been among them. The central charges are idolatry and abomination: great abominations in the sanctuary, idols portrayed in a hidden chamber, estrangement from the LORD through idols, not walking in his statutes while following the ordinances of surrounding nations, and filling Jerusalem with the slain. They defiled the land and profaned the holy name among the nations. They quote the sour grapes proverb and accuse the LORD of an unfair way, but he answers that their own way is unfair and that he will judge each according to his ways. They lament that their sins are upon them and that hope is lost. Signs, a riddle and parable are given to them, and they are told of exile, scattering among the nations, and eating unclean bread. Their reliance on Egypt proved a broken reed. The account then turns toward restoration. The LORD calls them to return, cast away transgressions and make a new heart and spirit. He promises to gather them, cleanse them from idols and filthiness, replace the stony heart, put his Spirit in them, and bring them to the land given to their fathers. The dry bones are identified with the whole house, which will become one nation under one king, with no more division into two kingdoms. A horn will sprout for Israel, and a good cedar is promised. They will remember their evil and loathe themselves, no longer defile the holy name, be shown the house and its pattern, and be accepted. The records end with the whole house receiving a city possession, 5,000 by 25,000, beside the holy portion, with land allotted by tribes and atonement made through the prince's offerings.

l: fathers (of the children of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The fathers of the children of Israel repeatedly rebelled against the LORD in Egypt and the wilderness, clinging to idols, rejecting ordinances and profaning Sabbaths. The LORD spared them from destruction but barred them from the land; later they worshipped at high places, called Bamah.

l: scroll (the scroll Ezekiel eats), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A scroll held out by a hand, written within and without with lamentations, mourning, and woe. The LORD then gives it to Ezekiel to eat; it tastes sweet as honey, and eating it precedes his commission to speak the LORD's words to Israel.

l: rebellion, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Rebellion marks the children of Israel and their fathers, who have transgressed against the speaker to this very day, and the people are repeatedly called a rebellious house, even 'most rebellious.' The son of man is warned not to be rebellious like that house. Their rebellion does not prevent the prophet's message from being sent.

l: watchman role, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The watchman is a role the LORD assigns to Ezekiel over the house of Israel. He must hear the LORD's word and warn the wicked and righteous; failure makes him answerable for blood, while warning that goes unheeded frees his own soul.

l: the wicked, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_fate die in his iniquity [when told 'You will surely die'] When the LORD says a wicked person will surely die, the watchman must warn him to turn from his wicked way. If Ezekiel gives no warning, the wicked man dies in his iniquity and the LORD requires his blood from Ezekiel. If warned and he does not turn, he dies in his iniquity but Ezekiel is free of blame.

l: the righteous, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_fate live [if he takes warning and does not sin] If a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, and the LORD lays a stumbling block before him, he will die, and his former righteous deeds will not be remembered. If Ezekiel fails to warn him, the LORD will require his blood at Ezekiel's hand. If Ezekiel warns him and he does not sin, he will surely live and Ezekiel has delivered his soul.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Jerusalem is the city at the center of these records, set by the LORD in the middle of the nations and belonging to him through covenant. It is a fortified city in Judah and holds the LORD's temple. It is portrayed as a person of foreign origin (Amorite father, Hittite mother), and as the younger sister Oholibah to Oholah, with Samaria and Sodom as sisters. Its story is one of favor, betrayal and judgment. The records open with Jerusalem portrayed on a tile and symbolically besieged, its bread supply to be broken. She is told she rebelled against the LORD's ordinances more than the nations, defiled the sanctuary, and will suffer unprecedented judgment, becoming a desolation and reproach, with only a remnant scattered. In visions Ezekiel is brought to the temple and sees idolatry in the gate, court and precincts. The city is full of blood and perversion; its people claim the LORD has forsaken the land. The wicked counsel of twenty-five men and the multiplied slain make the city a cauldron, and the LORD's glory departs from its midst. Four severe judgments (sword, famine, evil animals, pestilence) are sent, yet a remnant is carried out. An allegory describes her birth, being cast out naked, then saved, adorned and made the LORD's own; she trusted her beauty, prostituted herself with nations, and killed her children for idols, becoming more corrupt than Samaria and Sodom, though restoration and an everlasting covenant are promised. She lusts after Assyrians and Babylonians, is alienated from the latter, and drinks her sister's cup. She is called the bloody city that makes idols and profanes the Sabbaths. The Babylonian sword is aimed at her, with battering rams, mounds and forts, and the king of Babylon draws near on the very day the LORD speaks. Her sanctuary is profaned and her sons and daughters fall by the sword. Tyre gloats over her ruin as the former gateway of the peoples. The records end with an escapee reaching Ezekiel in the twelfth year of the captivity to report the city has been defeated.

l: siege of Jerusalem (tile depiction), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A symbolic enactment of Jerusalem's siege on a tile, serving as a sign to the house of Israel: forts, a mound, camps, and battering rams surround it, an iron pan stands as a wall, and the man faces it, arm bared, prophesying.

l: iniquity (of Israel and Judah), The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_duration 390 years for Israel [appointed as a number of days] The iniquity of the house of Israel is to be borne for 390 days, a day for each appointed year, and that of the house of Judah for 40 days. In the end, the people lack bread and water, are dismayed with one another, and pine away in their iniquity.

l: bread (mixed-grain bread), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A mixed-grain bread of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt, made in one vessel and eaten by Ezekiel for 390 days in rationed portions. Baked as barley cakes over dung, changed from human to cow's after protest, it symbolizes Israel's unclean bread and Jerusalem's broken staff.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Israel, also called the children of Israel and the house of Israel, is both a people and a land belonging to the LORD. The records portray it as a chosen but rebellious covenant people whose story moves from judgment through scattering to restoration. Early on, Israel (with Judah) is judged to have exceedingly great iniquity. It has a lewd heart that departed from God, plays the prostitute after idols, practices child sacrifice to this day, and rebelled in Egypt and the wilderness. It profaned the Sabbaths, was led astray by false prophets proclaiming peace where there was none, and desires to be like the nations. The people say the LORD has forsaken the land. The LORD calls the house of Israel dross, like bronze, tin, iron, and lead left over from silver, to be melted in the furnace of his wrath in Jerusalem. The land is to be desolate. Its dead will lie before its idols, many will fall by sword, famine, and pestilence, and a remnant will be scattered among the nations, as sworn in the wilderness. Its prince is called a deadly wounded wicked one, and the kingdom is to be overturned. The turn comes with the LORD's promise to gather the scattered flock. Neighbors such as Ammon and Edom rejoiced over Israel's desolate inheritance and mocked its mountains, and the LORD will answer on its behalf. Israel will be his instrument of vengeance on Edom. He will free it from scornful neighbors, bring it back from the sword and from many peoples to the mountains of Israel, and give it the land given to Jacob. There the people will dwell securely, building houses and planting vineyards. They will come to know that the LORD is their God and they are his people. The restored Israel dwells in unwalled villages with livestock and goods, which draws Gog's plan to plunder it. Israel instead burns the fallen army's weapons for seven years and buries Gog's multitude for seven months in the valley of Hamon Gog to cleanse the land. Its captivity, which came because of iniquity, is reversed. It receives mercy, forgets its shame, and receives the Lord's Spirit. The records end with order restored. Israel is rebuked for bringing uncircumcised foreigners into the sanctuary and is taught the difference between holy and common. The twelve tribes divide the land by lot, with Joseph receiving two portions, and aliens living among them are treated as native-born and given an inheritance.

l: nations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_attribute rejected God's ordinances [as stated of the surrounding countries] The nations surround Jerusalem, and the Lord says she has been more wicked and turbulent than they, though they themselves rejected His ordinances and did not walk in His statutes. They will witness the Lord's judgments on Jerusalem in the sight of all who pass by. Jerusalem will become a reproach, taunt, instruction and astonishment to them.

l: sword (the sword of judgment), The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_part_of God's judgment and wrath [a third will fall by the sword] The sword appears first as the prophet's razor and the instrument for striking a third of the hair around the city. It then stands for the Lord's judgment: a third of the people will fall by the sword around Jerusalem, and the Lord will draw out a sword after the scattered third. At the end He promises to bring the sword on her.

l: hair (the prophet's hair), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The prophet's shaved hair serves as a sign-act symbolizing Jerusalem. Weighed and divided in thirds, one part is burned, one struck with the sword, one scattered to the wind. A few strands are bound in his robe, some thrown into fire, which spreads to all Israel.

l: famine, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Famine is an evil arrow of destruction sent by God, part of His judgment and wrath. In Jerusalem it consumes a third of the people with pestilence; God promises to increase it, break their staff of bread, and lists it first among His sent punishments.

l: sword, famine, and pestilence, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Sword, famine, and pestilence are instruments of the Lord GOD's wrath on Israel. Chapter 6 assigns them by place: pestilence for the far off, sword for the near, famine for the besieged. Chapter 14 names four severe judgments, adding evil animals, and says the LORD will send all four on Jerusalem.

l: God's judgment and wrath, The Book of Ezekiel
s: God's judgment and wrath on Jerusalem: unprecedented, never to be repeated, because of her abominations and defiled sanctuary. He shows no pity or sparing until His anger is accomplished, making her a reproach among nations and teaching that the LORD spoke in zeal.

l: abominations and defilement of the sanctuary, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Abominations and defilement of the sanctuary denote Israel's idolatry and its pollution of God's holy name, which is evil and drives God far from his sanctuary. In Chapter 6 idolatry is a lewd, departing heart and worship on high hills, causing coming judgment and self-loathing among survivors. In Chapter 8 Ezekiel sees escalating abominations: the image of jealousy, hidden idols, weeping for Tammuz, and sun worship, alongside violence filling the land. In Chapter 43 prostitution, kings' dead bodies, and thresholds set beside God's create a wall and bring consuming anger; Israel must remove them so God may dwell among them forever.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The temple is the LORD's house, a walled, east-facing sanctuary with an outer court, an inner court, an east gate, a porch, a nave and an altar before the house. Its porch is twenty cubits long and eleven wide, with posts five cubits on each side. The temple is one hundred cubits long, and its walls are decorated with cherubim alternating with palm trees. It has two doors, each with two turning leaves. Most important, it is the place of the throne of the God of Israel and the soles of his feet, and its whole limit on the mountain top is most holy. The records unfold in stages. First, the house is shown defiled by idolatry at its north gate, inner court and temple door, which drives the Lord far from his sanctuary. Next, the cloud and brightness fill the house, and the glory leaves the threshold and stops at the east gate. Then the building is measured in detail, including porch, gate, temple, walls and doors. The glory returns by the east gate and fills the house, and its form and laws are to be written for Israel. Finally, waters flow eastward from under the threshold, making the temple the source of a river that gives life to trees.

l: mountains of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The mountains of Israel, with hills, watercourses and valleys, are addressed by the Lord GOD in prophecy. In Chapter 6 they face judgment: a sword comes and the slain lie among idols on the high places. In Chapter 36, having borne the nations' mockery and shame, they are promised restoration: branches, fruit, tilling, inhabitants, and an end to bereaving their nation, becoming Israel's inheritance. In Chapter 39 they are the site where Gog and his hordes fall, and where the great sacrifice feeds birds and animals.

l: idols (Israel's idols), The Book of Ezekiel
s: will_be broken Israel's idols will be broken and cease, and the slain will be cast down and the bones scattered before and around them. They are the objects after which the people's eyes play the prostitute and to which pleasant aroma was offered.

l: high places (of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: will_become desolate The Lord GOD says he will destroy the high places and that they will be desolate. They are linked to the altars and incense altars that will be laid waste, broken, and cut down.

l: remnant (of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A remnant of Israel escapes the sword and is scattered among the nations. In captivity they remember the Lord, recognize how their idolatrous hearts grieved him, loathe themselves for their abominations, and come to know he is the LORD.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The land of Israel is a place given by the LORD to the fathers of Israel and to Jacob, meant as an everlasting dwelling for the people and their descendants. The records trace it from judgment to restoration to ordered division. At the start it is told that the end has come on its four corners; it is full of bloody crimes and violence, and its houses and holy places will be profaned by the worst of the nations. Its inhabitants claim it as their possession, but the LORD promises it to the gathered exiles, who will remove its detestable things. Because of the abominations and violence of its people, the LORD vows to make it a desolation and an astonishment, its pride of power ended and its mountains empty of travelers, so that people will know he is the LORD. Those in the waste places still claim it as their inheritance. Having been defiled and made desolate, with the nations claiming it, it is then promised renewal: tilled, free from famine, cities inhabited and ruins rebuilt, so that it is called like the garden of Eden. The LORD will bring his people up from their graves, gather them from the nations, and make them one nation on the mountains of Israel. Finally the land is apportioned by lot among the twelve tribes, with Joseph holding two portions, and also to aliens living among them. An offering of 25,000 by 10,000 reeds, holy in all its border, holds the sanctuary, the priests' and Levites' portions, and lies beside the city possession. A southern border runs from Tamar to Meribath Kadesh, the brook, and the great sea.

l: the end (coming doom), The Book of Ezekiel
s: falls_on land of Israel [on its four corners] The end is announced repeatedly as a unique disaster that has come, awakes against the land, and is near, a day of tumult rather than joyful shouting. The rod has blossomed and pride has budded, and the vision concerns the whole multitude, so none will return or remain.

l: abominations and iniquity, The Book of Ezekiel
s: are_brought_on inhabitants of Israel [as judgment] The abominations of the people are to be brought on them and will be among them as part of the LORD's judgment. The people made images of their abominations and detestable things in the ornament of beauty the LORD had set in majesty, so he has made it unclean to them.

l: inhabitants of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: will_be_unable_to_be_saved_by silver and gold [in the day of the LORD's wrath] The inhabitants are warned that their doom has come, and they are to be judged according to their ways. Buyer and seller alike face wrath, no one goes to battle despite the trumpet, and survivors moan on the mountains with feeble hands, sackcloth, shame, and baldness. They seek peace and a vision from the prophet but find none, as the law perishes from the priest and counsel from the elders, and the king and prince mourn.

l: strangers and wicked nations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A group of strangers and wicked nations, called the terrible of the nations, whom the LORD brings as instruments of judgment. First they plunder and profane the ornament, houses and secret place; later they are sent against Tyre's prince, defiling his brightness and bringing him to a violent death.

l: prince in Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A prince in Jerusalem, subject of the LORD's burden, who flees in darkness through a hole in the wall with covered face. The LORD snares him in a net and brings him to Babylon, where he dies unseeing, clothed with desolation, his helpers and bands scattered.

l: Judah, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Judah is a tribal territory and people, bordering Reuben's portion and having a city gate on its north side. It is mocked and resented by neighboring nations (Ammon, Moab, Seir, Edom) after captivity, then is joined with Joseph's stick, symbolizing the end of division between two nations.

l: image of jealousy, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The image of jealousy is an object in Jerusalem, standing at the north-facing door of the inner court gate by the altar gate's entry; it provokes jealousy and is the first great abomination shown to Ezekiel.

l: seventy elders of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Seventy elders of the house of Israel, led by Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing among them, worship portrayed idols and creeping things on the wall, each holding a censer in the dark, claiming the LORD does not see them and has forsaken the land.

l: women weeping for Tammuz, The Book of Ezekiel
s: sits_at door of the gate of the LORD’s house toward the north [weeping for Tammuz] Ezekiel sees women sitting at the door of the north gate of the LORD's house weeping for Tammuz. The Lord names this as an abomination and says greater ones are still to come.

l: twenty-five men sun worshipers, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A group of about twenty-five men stands in the inner court between the porch and the altar at the LORD's temple door, backs to the temple, facing east, worshiping the sun.

l: idols and creeping things (portrayed on the wall), The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_located_at hidden room behind hole in the wall [portrayed around on the wall] Through a hole Ezekiel dug in the wall and a door beyond it, he sees every form of creeping things, abominable animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel portrayed around the wall. The seventy elders stand before them offering incense.

l: God's wrath and judgment, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_directed_at house of Judah [no sparing, no pity, no hearing of cries] The Lord declares he will deal in wrath, his eye will not spare, and he will have no pity. Though the people cry in his ears with a loud voice, he will not hear them.

l: man clothed in linen, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A figure dressed in linen who carries a writer's inkhorn and is counted among six men called executioners. He stands by the bronze altar, is told to mark the foreheads of those in Jerusalem who sigh over abominations, and reports the task done. Then he is sent between the wheels, takes fire from the cherub's hand, and goes out.

l: six men (the executioners), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Six armed executioners arrive from the upper gate in the north, each holding a slaughter weapon, and stand by the bronze altar. Ordered to follow the man in linen and kill without pity, sparing those marked, they begin with the old men before the house, then strike through the city.

l: mark, The Book of Ezekiel
s: protects men who sigh and cry [set on their foreheads; those marked are not to be approached by the killers] The mark is set on the foreheads of the men who sigh and cry over the abominations in the city, by the man clothed in linen. The six men are commanded not to come near anyone on whom the mark is found.

l: men who sigh and cry, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_disposition grief over abominations [over all the abominations done within Jerusalem] These men sigh and cry over all the abominations done within Jerusalem. The LORD orders them marked on the forehead, which sets them apart so that the executioners do not come near them.

l: slaughter of the city, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A slaughter of the city carried out by six men, beginning at the old men before the house and killing old, young, virgins, children and women, except the marked, filling the courts; the narrator protests, and the LORD cites the people's iniquity and bloodshed.

l: coals of fire, The Book of Ezekiel
s: located_at between the cherubim The man clothed in linen is told to take coals of fire from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city. A cherub stretches out his hand to the fire between the cherubim, takes some, and puts it into the man's hands.

l: Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Pelatiah, son of Benaiah, is a prince of the people seen among twenty-five men at the east gate with Jaazaniah; he dies while Ezekiel prophesies.

l: twenty-five men, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A group of twenty-five men stands at the east gate door of the LORD's house, devising iniquity and giving wicked counsel in the city. They dismiss building houses, calling the city a cauldron and themselves the meat. The LORD declares he will bring them out, deliver them to strangers, and judge them by the sword at Israel's border.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem are a group who tell Ezekiel's brothers and Israel to stay far from the LORD, claiming the land as their possession. Their unfaithfulness desolates the land, and they eat in fearfulness. Likened to useless vinewood, they face the LORD's set face and fire, and will know he is the LORD.

l: Chaldea, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Babylonians (Chaldeans) are men portrayed on a wall in red whom Oholibah lusts after and sends messengers to, and who come to her bed and defile her. She becomes alienated from them, and the LORD promises to bring them with the Assyrians against her with weapons, chariots, and a company of peoples to judge her.

l: cauldron and meat saying, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a saying of the twenty-five men [claims the city is the cauldron and they are the meat] The twenty-five men say, 'This is the cauldron, and we are the meat,' while dismissing the time for building houses. The LORD reverses it, saying their slain are the meat and the city the cauldron, and that the men will not be the meat but will be brought out and judged at the border of Israel.

l: Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Babylon, a Chaldean land ruled by King Nebuchadnezzar, is a city of merchants where Jerusalem's king and princes were brought, and where the LORD will judge the rebel king, who will die there.

l: exile, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Exile is what Ezekiel's actions portray, as he goes out at evening like men going into exile. The LORD says the house of Israel will go into exile and captivity, dispersed among the nations and scattered through the countries. A few will be left from sword, famine, and pestilence to declare their abominations among the nations.

l: baggage (Ezekiel's baggage), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Ezekiel prepares baggage for moving, brings it out by day in the sight of the people, and then carries it out on his shoulder in the dark through a hole dug in the wall. It serves as the physical prop of the sign, matching what the prince will do when he leaves with his baggage.

l: sign act of moving out, The Book of Ezekiel
s: symbolizes prince in Jerusalem [the burden concerns him and the house of Israel] The sign act is Ezekiel's moving out in the sight of the people, with baggage by day, a wall dug through in the evening, and his face covered. He does as commanded, and the LORD explains in the morning that it means, 'I am your sign. As I have done, so will it be done to them.' It foretells the exile of the prince and the people.

l: proverb about prolonged days and failing visions, The Book of Ezekiel
s: states the days are prolonged and every vision fails [current in the land of Israel] The proverb in the land of Israel says, 'The days are prolonged, and every vision fails.' The LORD says he will make it cease so it is no longer used in Israel. He replaces it with the declaration that the days are at hand and the fulfillment of every vision is near.

l: fulfillment of the LORD's word, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_near every vision [no more deferred] The LORD declares that the days are at hand for the fulfillment of every vision, with no more false vision or flattering divination in Israel. He says the word he speaks will be performed and will no longer be deferred, but will be carried out in the days of the rebellious house. He repeats that none of his words will be delayed any more.

l: false prophets of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The false prophets of Israel are a group who prophesy from their own heart and spirit, having seen nothing, yet claim 'The LORD says' though he has not sent them. Compared to foxes in waste places, they failed to go up into the gaps and build up the wall, instead seducing the people with 'Peace' where there is none and plastering a whitewashed wall. The LORD declares himself against them: they will be consumed when the wall falls and lose their place in the council, register, and land of Israel.

l: women who prophesy (daughters of your people), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A group of women who prophesy from their own hearts, not from the LORD. They sew magic bands and make veils to hunt souls, profane the LORD for barley and bread, and use lies to kill and spare wrongly. The LORD vows to tear off their bands and veils, free the ensnared souls, and end their false visions.

l: whitewashed wall, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A wall built by the people and whitewashed by false prophets, symbolizing false assurance of peace. The LORD declares a storm of wind, shower and hailstones will topple it, exposing its foundation, consuming its plasterers, and leaving both wall and plasterers no more.

l: storm of judgment, The Book of Ezekiel
s: consists_of stormy wind, overflowing shower and great hailstones [sent in the LORD's wrath] The LORD announces a stormy wind, an overflowing shower and great hailstones as the instruments of his wrath and anger against the whitewashed wall. The storm will tear down the wall, bring it to the ground, and consume the false prophets in the midst of it, so that they will know he is the LORD.

l: false visions and lying divination, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_claimed_falsely_as the LORD's word [the LORD has not spoken] The prophets and the women are charged with seeing falsehood and speaking lying divination, claiming the LORD's authority when he has not spoken. These false visions led people to hope that the word would be confirmed and to believe in peace. The LORD promises that the women will no more see false visions or practice divination, and that his hand will be against the prophets who utter them.

l: magic bands and veils, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_opposed_by the LORD [will tear them away and free the souls] The women sew magic bands on all elbows and make veils for the heads of people of every stature in order to hunt souls. The LORD says he is against the bands, will tear them from the women's arms, and will tear the veils. He will let the ensnared souls fly free like birds and deliver his people out of the women's hands.

l: elders of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Elders of Israel repeatedly come and sit before the prophet to inquire of the LORD. In Chapter 14 the LORD says they hold idols in their hearts and questions being inquired of by them; in Chapter 20 he rejects their inquiry, swearing he will not be inquired of.

l: idols, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Idols are taken into the hearts of Israelites and become the stumbling block of their iniquity. The LORD says he will answer idolatrous inquirers according to the multitude of their idols, and calls Israel to turn from them.

l: prophet (who is inquired of), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The prophet is the one to whom idolatrous men come to inquire. If a prophet is deceived and speaks a word, the LORD says he himself deceived him and will stretch out his hand to destroy him, so that the prophet's iniquity matches that of the one who seeks him.

l: Noah, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a righteous man [delivers only own soul by righteousness] Noah is named as one of three righteous men who, if present in a sinning land under judgment, would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness. They would save neither sons nor daughters.

l: Daniel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a righteous man [delivers only own soul by righteousness] Daniel is named alongside Noah and Job as a righteous man. If in a land facing famine, evil animals, sword, or pestilence, he would deliver only his own soul and not any sons or daughters.

l: Job, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a righteous man [delivers only own soul by righteousness] Job is named with Noah and Daniel as a righteous man whose righteousness would save only himself in a land under the LORD's judgment, not his children.

l: sinful land, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A land that sins by trespass is hypothetically struck by the LORD, who breaks its bread supply and cuts off man and animal through famine, evil animals, sword, or pestilence. Even the presence of three righteous men would not spare it; only they would be delivered while the land became desolate.

l: remnant, The Book of Ezekiel
s: comforts Ezekiel (son of man) [by their way and doings] A remnant of sons and daughters will be left in Jerusalem and carried out of it. They will come to the speaker's audience, and when their way and doings are seen, the audience will be comforted and know the LORD acted with cause.

l: vine tree, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The vine tree is one of the forest trees but proves worthless: its wood is useless for any work, even whole, not even a pin. Burned as fuel, the fire devours both ends and middle. It serves as the comparison for Jerusalem's inhabitants.

l: fire, The Book of Ezekiel
s: devours inhabitants of Jerusalem [even after they go out from the fire] The fire devours the vine wood at both ends and in the middle, leaving it burned and even less useful. The LORD says he has given the vine wood to the fire and will likewise give the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Though they go out from the fire, it will still devour them.

l: land, The Book of Ezekiel
s: becomes desolate [by the LORD's action] The LORD says he will make the land desolate. The reason given is that the inhabitants have acted unfaithfully.

l: Samaria, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Samaria, represented as Oholah, is the elder sister of Oholibah (Jerusalem). Belonging to the LORD, she nonetheless practiced spiritual prostitution from Egypt onward, lusting after Assyrians and defiling herself with idols, child sacrifice, a defiled sanctuary and profaned Sabbaths. The LORD delivered her to her Assyrian lovers, who took her children and killed her with the sword, making her a byword. Yet her sins were under half of Jerusalem's, and her captivity will be reversed.

l: Sodom, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Sodom is Jerusalem's younger sister, whose pride, fullness of bread, prosperous ease and neglect of the poor and needy, with arrogance and abomination, led the Lord GOD to remove it; Jerusalem did worse, yet Sodom's captivity will be reversed and it will be restored.

l: Egyptians, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Egyptians are scattered among the nations for forty years, then gathered and returned to Pathros, their birth land, as the lowest of kingdoms, coming to know the LORD because they had been a reed staff to Israel.

l: Philistines, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Philistines are accused of vengeful, perpetual hostility and contempt of soul; the LORD will stretch out his hand, cut off the Cherethites, destroy the sea coast's remnant, and execute great vengeance with wrathful rebukes.

l: Assyrians, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Assyrians are the neighboring lovers, governors, rulers and horsemen, on whom Oholah doted and with whose idols she defiled herself. The LORD delivers Oholah into their hand, and they kill her and take her children; Oholibah also lusts after them, and they are named among the forces that will come against her.

l: Jerusalem's lovers, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Jerusalem's lovers, including Egyptians, Assyrians and Chaldeans, were paid with her gifts and bribes; the Lord GOD will gather them against her to expose, strip, stone, stab and burn her.

l: idols and images, The Book of Ezekiel
s: are_made_from God's gold and silver jewels [made by Jerusalem] Jerusalem made high places and images of men from the garments and gold and silver jewels the Lord GOD gave her. She set his oil, incense, and bread before them and sacrificed her children to them. The blood of her children given to these idols is named as a reason for judgment.

l: covenant between God and Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A covenant the Lord GOD made with Jerusalem when he covered her nakedness and she became his; she despised the oath and broke it, yet he promises to remember it and establish an everlasting covenant, so she knows he is the LORD.

l: Jerusalem's prostitution (idolatry), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Jerusalem's prostitution is a metaphor for idolatry and unfaithfulness: she built high places on every street, offered herself to Egyptians, Assyrians, and Chaldeans, paid her lovers, was insatiable, and sacrificed sons and daughters through fire. Her filthiness and idols ground the judgment.

l: Judgment on Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Lord GOD's judgment on Jerusalem treats her like adulterous, bloodshedding women: her lovers strip her, destroy her high places, stone and stab her, and burn her houses, ending her prostitution and satisfying his wrath and jealousy, then restoration and forgiveness follow.

l: great eagle (first, Babylon's king), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A symbolic great eagle with large wings and multicolored feathers, representing Babylon's king. In Chapter 17 it takes the cedar's top twig to a merchant city, plants seed in fertile soil, and symbolizes the king taking Jerusalem's king and princes and covenanting with a royal offspring.

l: great eagle (second, Pharaoh), The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_feature great wings and many feathers The second great eagle, with great wings and many feathers, is the one toward whom the vine bends its roots and branches so that he might water it. In the interpretation, Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company will not help the rebel king in the war.

l: cedar (Lebanon's cedar), The Book of Ezekiel
s: located_in Lebanon The top of Lebanon's cedar is taken by the first great eagle, who crops off its topmost young twig. Later the LORD himself says he will take some of the cedar's lofty top and plant a tender twig on a high mountain.

l: vine (planted by the eagle), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A low, spreading vine planted by the eagle in good soil beside many waters to bear fruit. It first turns its branches toward the first eagle, then bends toward a second; the LORD warns it will be uprooted and wither utterly in the east wind.

l: Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Egypt is a land and nation, chiefly a place, whose story runs from Israel's past there to its own judgment. Early on, it is where the LORD made himself known to Israel and swore to bring them out to a good land; Israel did not forsake Egypt's idols, yet the LORD acted for his name's sake and led them out. It is also where two sisters first played the prostitute in youth, and Oholibah later lusts after the Egyptians until the LORD says she will stop remembering Egypt. Egypt is called a staff of reed to the house of Israel. The weight of the records falls on judgment: a sword cuts off man and animal, leaving desolation and waste from Seveneh to the border of Ethiopia. Its allies Ethiopia, Put, Lud, Cub and mixed peoples fall with it, and its cities, including Memphis, Pathros, Zoan, No, Sin and Tehaphnehes, are struck. Its pride is brought to nothing, its people scattered, and it is given to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for his army. It is later restored in Pathros as the lowest of kingdoms, and its waters run clear, so that they know the LORD is the LORD.

l: Judah's king (Zedekiah, royal offspring), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A royal offspring of Judah taken by Babylon's king, bound by covenant and oath so the kingdom would stay low but stand. He rebelled by sending ambassadors to Egypt for horses and many people. The LORD declares he will not escape, will be snared, and will die in Babylon; his fugitives fall by the sword.

l: covenant and oath with Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A covenant and oath the king of Babylon made with a royal offspring to keep the kingdom low and standing, not lifting itself up. Judah's king Zedekiah despised and broke it by seeking Egypt's help; the LORD claims it as his own and vows to bring it on his head.

l: tender twig (planted on Israel's mountain), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A tender twig, cropped by the LORD from the cedar's topmost young twigs, is planted on Israel's high mountain, where it will grow boughs and fruit, become a good cedar, and shelter birds of every kind.

l: sour grapes proverb (Israel's saying), The Book of Ezekiel
s: states fathers eat sour grapes and children's teeth are set on edge [implies children bear fathers' guilt] The proverb says that the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. The Lord GOD swears that Israel shall not use it any more, and the chapter answers it by teaching that each soul bears its own guilt.

l: righteous man (just man), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The righteous man does what is lawful and right: shuns idolatry, adultery and robbery, restores pledges, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, lends without interest, and keeps God's statutes, so he shall live. He fathers a robber son. The text warns that turning from righteousness to iniquity brings death.

l: wicked man, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The wicked man is a figure who stands under threat of death for his iniquity yet is offered a path to life. Across both chapters, the Lord takes no pleasure in the wicked's death and calls them to turn. If he turns from all sins, keeps the statutes, does what is lawful and right, restores pledges and returns robbed goods, he will surely live and his transgressions will not be remembered. If unwarned, he dies in iniquity, and the watchman is accountable.

l: robber son (son of the just man), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The robber son of a just man sheds blood, commits idolatry, adultery, oppression of the poor and usury, all called abominations. His father's righteousness cannot save him; he shall surely die, his blood upon him.

l: righteous grandson (son of the robber), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The righteous grandson, son of the robber, sees his father's sins, fears, and refuses to imitate them. He lives justly, feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and refusing interest and robbery, and so surely lives, while his father dies in his own iniquity.

l: individual responsibility for sin, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Individual responsibility for sin holds that the soul who sins shall die, while son and father do not bear each other's iniquity. Righteousness and wickedness rest on each person alone, and the Lord GOD defends this as fair against Israel's complaints.

l: repentance and return, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Repentance and return is God's call, since he has no pleasure in death. A wicked person who turns from all transgressions and does what is lawful and right shall live, unremembered sins; Israel must cast away transgressions and make a new heart and spirit.

l: individual responsibility and repentance, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A principle, affirmed by the Lord GOD against claims of unfairness, that the LORD judges each person by his own ways. Past righteousness cannot save a sinner, nor past wickedness condemn one who turns. Warnings ignored leave blood on the hearer; the watchman who warns is free. All are called to turn and live.

l: princes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: are_delivered_to sword (the LORD's sword) [along with my people] The princes of Israel are the subject of the lamentation the speaker is told to take up. Their mother is described first as a lioness and then as a vine, and her fate stands for theirs.

l: lioness (mother of the princes), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A lioness, mother of the princes, couches among lions and nourishes her cubs; after her first cub is taken to Egypt and hope is lost, she raises another as a young lion.

l: first cub (young lion taken to Egypt), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The first cub, a young lion raised by the lioness, learns to catch prey and devours men. The nations hear of him, capture him in their pit, and bring him with hooks to Egypt.

l: second cub (young lion taken to Babylon), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The second cub is a young lion who learns to catch prey, devours men, knows palaces, lays waste cities, and desolates the land with roaring. The nations then net and cage him with hooks and bring him to the king of Babylon, silencing his voice on Israel's mountains.

l: nations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The nations are a hostile collective that, in Chapter 19, capture two young lions in turn: first trapping one in a pit and hooking him to Egypt, then netting and caging another and delivering him to Babylon's king.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The entity is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon and king of kings, presented as a military ruler whose sword is the LORD's instrument of judgment. He first appears at a parting of two ways, using divination with arrows, teraphim, and liver; his right-hand lot points to Jerusalem, where he is to set battering rams, mounds, and forts, while his sword may go to Rabbah of Ammon instead. The LORD then brings him from the north against Tyre with horses, chariots, horsemen, and a large army, to kill, build forts and a mound, break walls and towers, and enter its gates. His army's great service against Tyre brought no wages, so the LORD gives him Egypt's multitude, plunder, and prey as payment. Finally, he and his people, called the terrible of the nations, draw swords against Egypt; the LORD strengthens his arms and puts the LORD's sword in his hand, so Egypt's multitude falls.

l: vine (mother of the princes), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A vine, mother of the princes, once planted by many waters, fruitful and tall with strong branches fit for rulers' scepters. It was then plucked up in fury and cast down; the east wind dried its fruit, and fire consumed its broken branches. Now it sits in a dry, thirsty wilderness, with no strong branch left to rule.

l: lamentation for the princes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A lamentation for the princes of Israel, which the speaker is commanded to take up, told through images of a lioness with her cubs and a vine, ending as a lamentation.

l: wilderness, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The wilderness is where the LORD gave his statutes, ordinances and Sabbaths, and where Israel and then their children rebelled. There he swore not to bring that generation into the land and to scatter them later. He promises a future judgment "face to face" in the wilderness of the peoples, as he did with the fathers.

l: promised land (flowing with milk and honey), The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_described_as glory of all lands [flowing with milk and honey] The land is described as one the LORD searched out, flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands. The rebellious wilderness generation was denied entry, and rebels purged in the future will not enter it. The LORD promises to bring the gathered Israel into it, the country sworn to their fathers.

l: idols, The Book of Ezekiel
