s: Idols, including the idols of Egypt and of the fathers, are what Israel refused to throw away and followed with their hearts and eyes. The LORD says Israel's gifts and sacrifices to them profane his name, and he tells them in irony to go serve them, though they will no longer profane his name.

l: statutes and ordinances, The Book of Ezekiel
s: gives life [to the man who keeps them] The LORD gave statutes and ordinances by which a man who does them will live, and Israel repeatedly rejected them. He also says he gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances in which they could not live, and polluted them in their gifts, in the passing of firstborn through the fire.

l: forest of the south, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_target_of prophecy [Ezekiel told to prophesy against it] The forest of the south is the target of a prophecy: the LORD will kindle a fire in it that devours every green and dry tree. All faces from south to north will be burned.

l: fire (kindled in the southern forest), The Book of Ezekiel
s: consumes every green tree and every dry tree [kindled by the LORD, not quenched] The LORD says he will kindle a fire that devours every green tree and every dry tree and will not be quenched. All flesh will see that the LORD has kindled it.

l: judgment of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: takes_place_in wilderness of the peoples [face to face] The LORD will enter into judgment with Israel face to face in the wilderness of the peoples, as he did with their fathers. He will cause them to pass under the rod, bring them into the bond of the covenant, and purge out rebels, who will not enter the land of Israel.

l: gathering and return of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: leads_to land of Israel [LORD gathers them from the countries] The LORD promises to bring Israel out from the peoples and gather them from the countries where they are scattered, with a mighty hand and outstretched arm. He will bring them into the land, accept them on his holy mountain, and be sanctified in them before the nations. There they will remember and loathe their evil ways and know that he dealt with them for his name's sake.

l: sword (the LORD's sword), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The LORD's sword is a weapon drawn from its sheath, sharpened and polished to slaughter and flash like lightning, then handed to a killer. It is set against all gates, doubled to a third time, and will not return to its sheath for Israel, though the LORD later tells it to return for Ammon. It is identified with the Babylonian king's sword.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Ammon is a nation, the children of Ammon, whose city Rabbah is a target of the LORD's polished sword. Its people see false visions and divine lies, and they rejoice with contempt, saying 'Aha!' against the sanctuary, Israel, and Judah. The LORD declares judgment and vengeance: he will judge Ammon in the land of its birth, pour out indignation, and deliver it to brutish men and to the children of the east as a possession. Rabbah becomes a stable for camels and Ammon a resting place for flocks. Ammon is plundered, cut off, destroyed, and forgotten among the nations.

l: prince of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The prince of Israel is a wicked, deadly wounded figure whose day arrives in the time of the end's iniquity. The LORD orders his turban and crown removed, the low exalted and the high humbled. His rule is overturned and stays unrestored until the rightful one comes.

l: princes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The princes of Israel are accused in Jerusalem of shedding blood according to their power, likened to wolves ravening prey and destroying souls for dishonest gain.

l: prophets (Jerusalem's prophets), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Jerusalem's prophets are accused of conspiracy, likened to a roaring lion devouring souls, taking treasure and making widows, and whitewashing for leaders with false visions and lies, claiming 'The Lord GOD says' unspoken.

l: priests (Jerusalem's priests), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Jerusalem's priests are accused of violating God's law: they profane holy things, blur holy/common and unclean/clean distinctions, and ignore his Sabbaths, so the LORD is profaned among them.

l: people of the land, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The people of the land are accused of oppression and robbery, troubling the poor and needy and wrongfully oppressing the foreigner.

l: furnace, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The furnace serves as the image of judgment. As metals are gathered into its middle and melted by blown fire, so the LORD will gather Israel in Jerusalem and melt them in his anger and wrath.

l: dross, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a dross of silver Dross is the LORD's description of the house of Israel, who are like bronze, tin, iron, and lead, the dross of silver. Because they have all become dross, they will be gathered and melted.

l: bloodshed, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Bloodshed is the leading charge against the city, whose people shed blood within her, including through slander, bribes, and the princes' violence. It makes them guilty, and the LORD strikes his hand at the blood shed within her.

l: God's wrath, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_poured_out_on Israel [consuming them with fire] God's wrath is the fire the LORD will blow on Israel to melt them like metal in a furnace, so they will know he has poured it out. At the end, he says he has poured out his indignation, consumed them with the fire of his wrath, and brought their own way on their heads.

l: prostitution (spiritual unfaithfulness), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Prostitution is the text's image for the sisters' unfaithfulness to the LORD, through foreign alliances, lovers, and idols, which began in Egypt and continued in Samaria and Jerusalem. The LORD declares he will make it cease so that all women may be taught not to be lewd, and that they will bear the sins of their idols.

l: idols, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The sisters defile themselves with the idols of their lovers and commit adultery with them. They sacrifice the sons they bore to the LORD by making them pass through the fire to the idols, then enter the sanctuary the same day. Oholibah is told she will bear the sins of her idols.

l: cup of judgment (sister's cup), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A deep, large cup of drunkenness, sorrow, astonishment, desolation, ridicule and derision, Samaria's and Oholah's, which the LORD gives to Oholibah for walking her sister's way; she drains it, gnaws its pieces, tears her breasts.

l: judgment on Oholibah, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A judgment issued by the LORD against Oholibah, carried out by her alienated lovers, the Babylonians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians, who come against her on every side. They strip her, mutilate her, take her children, let the remnant fall by sword, burn the rest, and a mob stones her, ending her lewdness so she knows the Lord GOD.

l: rebellious house, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a audience of the parable [told to utter a parable to them] The rebellious house is the audience of the cauldron parable that Ezekiel is told to utter. They ask what his behavior means, and he tells them they will do as he has done, unable to mourn and pining away in their iniquities. When this comes, they will know that the LORD is the Lord GOD.

l: cauldron (parable of the cauldron), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The cauldron is a parable image of the bloody city, Jerusalem, whose stubborn rust never leaves it. It is filled with choice meat and bones and boiled, then set empty on coals so its filth melts away, showing no cleansing until the LORD's wrath rests.

l: Ezekiel's wife, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a desire of Ezekiel's eyes [taken away with one stroke] Ezekiel's wife is the desire of his eyes, whom the LORD says he will take away with one stroke. She dies at evening, after Ezekiel had spoken to the people that morning. Ezekiel does not mourn her publicly, as commanded.

l: mourning customs, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_rule no mourning [no covering lips, no mourner's bread, headdress and sandals kept on] Ezekiel is forbidden to weep, make mourning for the dead, cover his lips, or eat mourner's bread, and must keep his headdress and sandals on. This conduct becomes a sign of what the people will do when the sanctuary is profaned and their children die. They will not mourn or weep but will pine away in their iniquities and moan to one another.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_agent king of Babylon [drew close to Jerusalem on the day] The text says the king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem on the same day, in the ninth year, tenth month, tenth day, that the LORD's word came to Ezekiel. Ezekiel is told to write down that day. The cauldron parable portrays the coming fire and destruction of the city that follows.

l: children of the east, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The children of the east are to receive Ammon as a possession. They will set encampments and dwellings there, eat its fruit, and drink its milk. They will also be given access to Moab's frontier cities in order to go against Ammon.

l: Moab, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Moab is a nation with frontier cities Beth Jeshimoth, Baal Meon, and Kiriathaim, called the glory of the country. Accused, with Seir, of saying Judah is like all nations, it faces judgment: its frontier cities will be opened and given to the children of the east, so they will know the LORD.

l: Mount Seir, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Mount Seir, identified with all Edom, is a mountain targeted by the LORD's prophecy. Accused of perpetual hostility toward Israel, pursuit by blood, covetousness of Israel and Judah, and insulting Israel's mountains, it is sentenced to desolation. Its cities will be laid waste and uninhabited, and its hills, valleys, and watercourses filled with the slain.

l: Edom, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Edom is a nation and territory, spanning Teman to Dedan and linked with Mount Seir, accused of taking offending vengeance against Judah. Across the records it faces judgment: the LORD will cut off man and animal, leaving it desolate, and Israel will carry out his vengeance. Its kings and princes are later pictured slain by the sword in Sheol among the uncircumcised. The account ends with Edom, with Mount Seir, wholly desolate, so that they will know the LORD.

l: judgment and vengeance, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Judgment takes the form of the LORD's announced punishments on each nation, each introduced by 'because' and 'therefore' and ending with the recognition that he is the LORD. Vengeance appears in two ways: Edom and the Philistines are condemned for taking vengeance, and the LORD in turn lays his own vengeance on them, with Edom's carried out by Israel.

l: Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Tyre is a seafaring merchant city set at the entry of the sea, in the heart of the seas, renowned as strong and claiming perfect beauty. Its inhabitants trade with the peoples of many islands and enrich the kings of the earth. Chapter 26 condemns it for gloating over Jerusalem's fall; the Lord GOD declares his opposition, and its walls, towers and wealth will fall. Chapter 27 portrays its rich trade and brokenness by the seas. Chapter 28 addresses its prince and king, whose wisdom-gained wealth ends in destruction. Tyre becomes a bare rock for nets, descends to the pit, is never rebuilt, and is no more.

l: many nations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: come_up_against Tyre [like waves of the sea] Many nations will be caused to come up against Tyre as the sea causes its waves to rise. Tyre will become plunder for the nations.

l: Sheol, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Sheol is the place of the dead, called the pit and the lower parts of the earth. The LORD casts the Assyrian and his arm down there, mourning follows, and fallen nations lie uncircumcised, slain by the sword. The mighty speak from its middle, and Egypt's multitude is to be cast into it.

l: destruction of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Lord GOD brings Nebuchadnezzar from the north against Tyre; siege breaks its walls and towers, slays its people, plunders its riches, and casts it into the waters, leaving it a vanished terror lamented by the sea's princes.

l: lamentation over Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A lamentation the LORD commands Ezekiel to take up, portraying Tyre as a splendid ship and trading power, and ending with mourners asking who was like Tyre, now silenced in the sea.

l: ship of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Tyre is depicted as a magnificent ship built from materials gathered from many lands: Senir cypress planks, Lebanon cedar mast, Bashan oak oars, Kittim ivory benches, Egyptian embroidered linen sail, Elishah awning. Its rowers steer it into great waters, where the east wind wrecks it.

l: Sidon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Sidon is a place the LORD declares himself against; the prophet is told to prophesy against it, announcing pestilence, blood in its streets, and sword on every side, so they will know the LORD.

l: Tubal, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_located_in Sheol [graves around them, uncircumcised, slain by the sword] Tubal is named together with Meshech and their multitude, whose graves are around them, all uncircumcised and slain by the sword. They caused terror in the land of the living and do not lie with the mighty fallen with their weapons.

l: Meshech, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_located_in Sheol [graves around them, uncircumcised, slain by the sword] Meshech is in Sheol with all their multitude, their graves around them, all uncircumcised and slain by the sword for having caused terror in the land of the living. They do not lie with the fallen mighty who went down with their weapons of war. Their iniquities are on their bones.

l: Eden, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The garden of God is the place whose cedars could not hide the Assyrian cedar and whose cypress and pine trees were not like its branches. No tree there matched its beauty. The trees of Eden in the garden envied it, and later they are brought down to the lower parts of the earth and comforted there.

l: Asshur, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Asshur is depicted as a group, with her company, lying slain by the sword in the pit of Sheol, graves set around her, having once caused terror in the land of the living.

l: Tyre's trade and merchandise, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Tyre's trade and merchandise is a catalogue of the many nations that traded with Tyre. Tarshish paid silver, iron, tin, and lead; Javan, Tubal, and Meshech supplied persons and bronze vessels; Togarmah horses and mules; Judah and Israel wheat, honey, oil, and balm; Sheba and Raamah spices, stones, and gold. Others include Dedan, Syria, Damascus, Arabia, Kedar, and Vedan. This commerce filled many peoples and enriched the kings of the earth, but it ends in ruin, when the merchandise falls into the seas on the day of Tyre's fall.

l: Tyre's mariners and crew (Tyre), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Tyre's mariners and crew were drawn from Sidon, Arvad, Gebal and its own wise men, with an army of foreign men. When the ship falls, the mariners and pilots come ashore, weeping, wearing sackcloth, and mourning Tyre.

l: Tyre's downfall, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Tyre's downfall is a catastrophic ruin in the heart of the seas, caused by the east wind. Its riches, crew and wares sink; island inhabitants are astonished, kings terrified, and merchants hiss in mockery, as Tyre meets a terrible end and will be no more.

l: prince of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The prince of Tyre is a wise, wealthy trader whose riches make him proud. He falsely claims to be a god and sits in God's seat, though he is only a man. He is therefore condemned to die at strangers' hands, the death of the uncircumcised.

l: king of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The king of Tyre is the subject of a lamentation in Chapter 28. He is portrayed as an anointed cherub, perfect in beauty and wisdom, adorned with precious stones in Eden, set on God's holy mountain. Unrighteousness, pride, and violence from his commerce corrupted him. He was cast out as profane, consumed by fire from within, reduced to ashes before kings, and became a terror who will exist no more.

l: Ezekiel (son of man), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Ezekiel, repeatedly addressed by the LORD as "son of man," is a prophet and watchman set over the house of Israel. The records show him receiving the LORD's word and being commissioned to prophesy, with an earlier vision at the river Chebar. His role is to speak warnings, or else bear responsibility for the blood of the wicked. After a fugitive brings news of Jerusalem's defeat, his mouth is opened and he is no longer mute. The people flock to hear him as to a pleasant song but do not obey, and when the prophecy comes to pass they will know a prophet has been among them. He is then carried by the Spirit into the valley of bones, answers 'Lord GOD, you know,' and prophesies to the bones and the wind as commanded. He is told to write on two sticks and join them into one, explaining the meaning to the people. He is also commanded to set his face toward Gog and prophesy against him, twice, including that the LORD will bring Gog against Israel. In the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, he is brought in visions of God to a very high mountain in the land of Israel. He is told to see, hear, and set his heart on all that is shown, and to declare it to Israel. A guide leads him through the outer court, north rooms, and measurements of the area. He is brought to the east gate, sees the glory approach and fill the house, and falls on his face. The Spirit lifts him into the inner court, where he is commanded to show the house, its form and laws, to Israel, writing them in the people's sight, and to mark all ordinances for the rebellious house. The sequence ends with him led through the river at ankle, knee, and waist depth until it cannot be crossed, then seeing the many trees and hearing the healing effect explained.

l: judgment on Tyre and Sidon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The LORD pronounces judgment on Tyre's prince and king through foreign swords, death, a devouring fire, and ashes, and on Sidon through pestilence, bloodshed, and the sword. The purpose stated is that they will know he is the LORD and that he is sanctified, and the judgments also end the scorn Israel suffered from those around them.

l: pride and wealth from commerce, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The prince of Tyre's heart is lifted up because of riches gained by wisdom and trading, leading him to claim divinity. The king's abundant commerce filled him with violence and unrighteousness, profaned his sanctuaries, and led to his downfall.

l: Pharaoh king of Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is portrayed as a great monster lying in his rivers, boasting that the rivers are his own. The LORD stands against him in judgment. In the first account he is hooked, pulled out, and cast into the wilderness as food for animals and birds. Next he is compared in greatness to the proud Assyrian cedar and told he will be brought down with the trees of Eden to Sheol, lying among the uncircumcised slain by the sword. Finally he is lamented as a young lion of the nations and a monster in the seas who troubled the waters. He will be netted and laid among the slain, seeing other fallen nations and being comforted, since the LORD has put his terror in the land of the living.

l: forty years of desolation, The Book of Ezekiel
s: duration_of_desolation_of Egypt [uninhabited, no foot passes through] Egypt's land and cities are to be a desolation for forty years, uninhabited and unpassed by man or animal, while the Egyptians are scattered among the nations. At the end of the forty years the LORD will gather them and return them to Pathros.

l: multitude of Pharaoh, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The multitude of Pharaoh is the host of followers belonging to Egypt's king. First, Pharaoh's arm is shown broken by the LORD and unhealed, with both arms to be broken before Babylon's king. Then his multitude is joined to him in the Assyrian cedar comparison, sharing his coming fall to the lower parts of the earth.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The day of the LORD is a near day of clouds and a time of the nations, mourned with 'Alas for the day!'; it brings the sword on Egypt, anguish in Ethiopia, and allies' fall.

l: judgment on Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_purpose Egypt will know the LORD The LORD says he will execute judgments on Egypt through fire, sword and the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, ending its idols, its prince, and its multitude, and striking cities such as Memphis, Zoan, No and Sin. The purpose repeated is that they will know that he is the LORD. A second oracle adds the breaking of Pharaoh's arms and the scattering of the Egyptians among the nations.

l: Assyrian, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Assyrian is figuratively a tall, beautiful cedar in Lebanon, nourished by many waters, sheltering great nations. Its heart grew proud in its height, so the LORD delivered it to the mighty one of the nations; foreigners cut it down and it descended to Sheol with the slain.

l: cedar in Lebanon (the Assyrian), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The cedar in Lebanon is a beautiful, exalted tree with lovely branches, rooted by many deep waters, sheltering birds and animals. It surpassed every tree in the garden of God, whose trees envied it. It is finally cut down, its branches scattered across mountains and valleys, serving as a warning against self-exaltation.

l: fall of the Assyrian, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The Assyrian's fall, caused by pride and wickedness, comes when the LORD gives it to a mighty nation's hand and foreigners cut it off. Branches fall, peoples leave its shadow, and it is cast to Sheol. Nations shake, Lebanon mourns, and Pharaoh is warned.

l: Elam, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Elam is a slain, uncircumcised multitude lying in Sheol, the lower parts of the earth, around her grave; once a terror in the land of the living, she now bears shame with those in the pit.

l: princes of the north, The Book of Ezekiel
s: lie_with uncircumcised [slain by the sword, bearing shame] All the princes of the north have gone down with the slain. They are put to shame for the terror they caused by their might, lying uncircumcised with those slain by the sword and bearing their shame with those in the pit.

l: Sidonians, The Book of Ezekiel
s: lie_with uncircumcised [slain by the sword, bearing shame] All the Sidonians are named with the princes of the north as having gone down with the slain. They are put to shame in the terror they caused by their might and lie uncircumcised among those slain by the sword.

l: lamentation over Pharaoh, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_lamented_by daughters of the nations [over Egypt and all her multitude] The LORD commands Ezekiel to take up this lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt, comparing him to a young lion who is really a monster in the seas. The LORD says the daughters of the nations will lament with it over Egypt and all her multitude.

l: watchman (parable watchman), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A parable figure chosen by a land's people as watchman to blow the trumpet when the sword approaches. If warned people ignore him, their blood is on themselves; if he fails to warn, the LORD requires their blood from him. Ezekiel is told he is Israel's watchman.

l: the righteous, The Book of Ezekiel
s: dies_if turns to iniquity [trusting in his own righteousness] The righteous are told their past righteousness will not deliver them on the day they sin. If one trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered and he will die in his iniquity. This shows that the righteous who turn from righteousness will die therein.

l: inhabitants of the waste places, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A group living in the waste places of the land of Israel claims the land as inheritance, reasoning that if Abraham, one man, inherited it, they, being many, surely do. The LORD rebukes their blood-eating, idolatry, bloodshed, abominations and adultery, and declares they will die by sword, wild animals, or pestilence.

l: sword, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The sword is the instrument of judgment the LORD brings on a land, which the watchman must warn of by blowing the trumpet. It is said to take away those who ignore the warning. The LORD also declares that those in the waste places will fall by the sword.

l: shepherds of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: rule_over sheep (the LORD's flock, Israel) [with force and with rigor] The shepherds are condemned for feeding themselves, eating the fat and clothing themselves with wool, while failing to strengthen, heal, bind up, bring back, or seek the sheep, and instead ruling them with force and rigor. The LORD declares he is against them, will require his sheep from them, and will make them cease from feeding the sheep so that the flock is delivered from their mouth.

l: sheep (the LORD's flock, Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: belongs_to the LORD [my sheep, the sheep of my pasture] The sheep were scattered over the mountains and the whole earth for lack of a shepherd and became prey and food for the animals of the field. The LORD promises to rescue, gather, feed, and heal them, and to judge between fat and lean sheep, since the strong have trampled the pasture, fouled the water, and pushed the diseased away. They will dwell securely, no longer be prey, and know that the LORD is with them and they are his people, the sheep of his pasture.

l: David, The Book of Ezekiel
s: David is the LORD's servant, promised as the one shepherd over Israel, the LORD's flock. In Chapter 34 he is set up to feed the sheep and is named prince among them. In Chapter 37 the promise grows: he will be king over the united people and their prince forever, as they walk in the LORD's ordinances.

l: scattering and regathering of the flock, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_cause no shepherd [reason for the scattering] The flock was scattered through all the mountains, high hills, and the surface of the earth because there was no shepherd, and no one searched or sought for them. The LORD promises to deliver them from all places of the cloudy and dark day, bring them out from the peoples and countries into their own land, and feed them there in security.

l: perpetual hostility (Seir's hostility toward Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Seir's perpetual hostility is the first ground of the LORD's judgment, expressed in giving Israel over to the sword in its calamity. Because Seir did not hate blood, blood will pursue it, and the LORD will act according to its anger, envy, and hatred.

l: desolation (judgment on Seir), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The LORD pledges to make Mount Seir a desolation and an astonishment, a perpetual desolation with cities uninhabited and its land full of the slain. It is measured against Seir's own rejoicing over Israel's desolation: 'as you rejoiced... so I will do to you.' It extends to all Edom and leads them to know that the LORD is the LORD.

l: residue of the nations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The residue of the nations, with all Edom, seized Israel's land joyfully and spitefully, making it prey and derision. The Lord God, jealous, swears they will bear their shame, and those left around Israel will learn that the LORD rebuilt the ruins and replanted desolation.

l: cleansing of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: God promises to cleanse Israel by sprinkling clean water, removing filthiness and idols, replacing their stony heart with a new heart and spirit, and putting his Spirit within them, for his holy name's sake; they will loathe themselves, then cities are rebuilt.

l: scattering of Israel among the nations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: God scatters Israel among the nations, pouring out wrath for their bloodshed and idols and judging their deeds. Among the nations they profane his holy name, as people say they left the LORD's land. Out of respect for his name, God gathers them from all countries and returns them.

l: valley of bones, The Book of Ezekiel
s: contains dry bones [very many, very dry] The valley is where the LORD sets the prophet down, and it is full of very many dry bones in the open. There the bones are reassembled and raised to life as an exceedingly great army.

l: dry bones, The Book of Ezekiel
s: represents house of Israel [symbolic meaning given by the LORD] At the prophet's prophesying the dry bones come together bone to bone, gain sinews, flesh and skin, and then receive breath, live, and stand on their feet as an exceedingly great army. The LORD says they represent the whole house of Israel, who say their bones are dried up and their hope is lost.

l: breath (wind), The Book of Ezekiel
s: comes_from four winds [commanded to breathe on the slain so they live] The bones have no breath in them after receiving sinews, flesh and skin, so the prophet is told to prophesy to the wind to come from the four winds and breathe on the slain. The breath enters them and they live and stand up.

l: Joseph, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Joseph is a name tied to a stick held by Ephraim and a gate on the city's east side; the LORD promises to join Joseph's stick with Judah's stick, making them one in his hand.

l: sticks, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Two sticks, one inscribed for Judah and companions, one for Joseph/Ephraim, are written on by the prophet and joined into one in his hand, signifying the LORD will unite divided Israel into one nation.

l: Gog, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Gog is a prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, from the land of Magog, who leads an army and allied peoples. Prophets of Israel had long foretold that God would bring him against Israel. The LORD declares himself Gog's adversary, turns him around, hooks his jaws, and draws him from the far north to plunder Israel's unwalled villages. There, judgment falls on him and his hordes through sword, pestilence, blood, rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur. His bow and arrows are struck from his hands, and he and his multitude fall in the open field. They are buried in Israel, in the valley of Hamon Gog.

l: Gog's army and allied peoples, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Gog's army is a coalition of Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer with all his hordes, and Togarmah from the far north, with armored horses and horsemen, shields, and swords. They advance like a storm and cloud, but the LORD's judgment destroys them: swords turn on brothers, with rain, hailstones, fire, sulfur. Sheba, Dedan, Tarshish merchants question Gog's plunder motive.
